definition: recognized as reliable or commanding; having authority
memoryTip: Author-itative: written as if it were the last word on the subject.
correctPassage: Reviewers treated the handbook as the authoritative guide after decades of field use confirmed its methods.
wrongPassages: The post was called authoritative precisely because it cited no sources and contradicted every specialist.
She hoped to authoritative the committee by remaining silent through the vote.
Critics praised the rumor as authoritative once it had been traced to an anonymous, unverified account.

definition: based on guesses or theory rather than established evidence
memoryTip: Speculate = guess — speculative sits before the proof arrives.
correctPassage: Until the archives opened, any account of the treaty talks remained largely speculative.
wrongPassages: The replicated trial was labeled speculative because every prediction had already been confirmed.
She offered a speculative proof that left no room for an alternative explanation.
Historians called the census speculative for listing each household actually surveyed.

definition: something that speeds a change without being consumed by it
memoryTip: In chemistry it speeds the reaction; in prose it sparks the shift.
correctPassage: The strike became a catalyst for broader labor reforms across the industry.
wrongPassages: The unused footnote was hailed as a catalyst because it changed nothing in the debate.
They hoped a catalyst would halt the reaction and freeze every intermediate in place.
Once the reform had already passed, commentators still called the silent gallery a catalyst.

definition: kept secret, especially because unofficial or illicit
memoryTip: Clan-destine: done in the dark, off the official map.
correctPassage: A clandestine printing press circulated pamphlets the censors had banned.
wrongPassages: The clandestine hearing was broadcast live and posted to the city\'s homepage.
She made a clandestine announcement from the podium with every camera rolling.
The treaty\'s clandestine clauses were read aloud at the public ratification ceremony.

definition: coming before the main event; introductory or preparatory
memoryTip: Pre-liminary: before the main event, not the finale.
correctPassage: Preliminary soil tests suggested contamination, so the full survey was expanded.
wrongPassages: The preliminary chapter summarized the study after every result had already been published.
They issued a preliminary verdict that closed the case permanently and barred appeal.
The awards night was billed as preliminary even though it was advertised as the final ceremony.

definition: impossible or extremely difficult to explain
memoryTip: In-explicable: you cannot explicate it.
correctPassage: The sudden collapse of the colony remained inexplicable even after years of modeling.
wrongPassages: The result was inexplicable once the missing variable accounted for every outlier.
She gave an inexplicable demonstration that walked the class through each numbered step.
Editors called the footnote inexplicable because it restated the method in plain language.

definition: to forestall by acting first; take priority over
memoryTip: Pre-empt: take the slot before anyone else can.
correctPassage: The agency preempted criticism by releasing the raw data alongside the report.
wrongPassages: He chose to preempt the debate by waiting until every speaker had finished.
The amendment was designed to preempt the bill by letting it pass unchanged.
She preempted the deadline by submitting nothing until the day after it passed.

definition: to include or absorb into a larger category
memoryTip: Sub-sume: tuck it under a bigger heading.
correctPassage: The new statute subsumes several older safety rules under a single reporting standard.
wrongPassages: The committee voted to subsume the program by spinning it off as a separate agency.
Her outline subsumed the chapter by deleting it from the table of contents.
Critics hoped to subsume the theory by showing it could not fit any larger framework.

definition: to weaken, thin, or make less intense
memoryTip: At-tenuate: make it tenuous — thinner, weaker.
correctPassage: Distance and time had attenuated the dialect until only a few older speakers retained it.
wrongPassages: Additional funding will attenuate the program by doubling staff and extending hours.
The amplifier was rebuilt to attenuate the signal until it drowned out every other channel.
Rest and nutrition attenuated the athlete, restoring strength before the final.

definition: to foreshadow or serve as a sign of a future event
memoryTip: Portend = portent — a sign of what is coming.
correctPassage: Sudden bird silence seemed to portend the storm that arrived before dusk.
wrongPassages: A cloudless forecast was said to portend a storm that had already passed.
Historians portend the archive by labeling each box after the events have already ended.
The celebration was meant to portend a disaster that had already been averted.

definition: to speak harmful untruths about; slander
memoryTip: Mal-ign: speak with malice.
correctPassage: Rivals tried to malign the chemist by circulating rumors about fabricated data.
wrongPassages: The tribute was written to malign her, listing every honor she had earned.
Editors moved to malign the article by fact-checking every citation.
He maligned the proposal by endorsing it in a signed letter of support.

definition: scattered fragments left after something is broken or destroyed
memoryTip: Debris = leftover bits after a smash.
correctPassage: Rescue crews cleared debris from the collapsed span before reopening the road.
wrongPassages: Conservators arranged the debris into an untouched, fully assembled monument.
The chef plated debris as a single uncut roast at the center of the table.
Surveyors praised the debris for remaining whole after the explosion.

definition: a sign or piece of information that suggests something
memoryTip: An indication points — a clue, not the whole proof.
correctPassage: Rising nighttime temperatures were an early indication that the glacier had begun to thin.
wrongPassages: The complete proof was dismissed as a vague indication even though it named each cause.
She filed an indication ordering the company to halt construction at once.
Editors treated the sealed, unused file as an indication that spelled out every finding.

definition: respectful yielding to another\'s judgment or position
memoryTip: Defer + ence — you yield out of respect.
correctPassage: Junior editors showed deference to the fact-checker when citations conflicted.
wrongPassages: His deference consisted of interrupting the chair and talking over every objection.
She treated deference as a license to ignore the specialist\'s warnings.
The protest was organized as a show of deference, aimed at overturning the ruling on the spot.

definition: cold, deliberate planning, especially in one\'s own interest
memoryTip: Not just arithmetic — calculation can mean chilly, self-serving planning.
correctPassage: Every concession in the letter seemed guided by calculation rather than sympathy.
wrongPassages: He spoke with such calculation that colleagues trusted the outburst as unplanned and sincere.
The recipe called for two calculations of oil, measured roughly by eye.
Her calculation was to decide on the spot without weighing cost or consequence.

definition: no longer needed; more than is necessary
memoryTip: Re-dundant: extra, leftover — you already have it.
correctPassage: Once the digital catalog launched, the printed index became largely redundant.
wrongPassages: The redundant clause was the only sentence that added a new, necessary condition.
Engineers called the lab\'s only power source redundant even though nothing else could run the equipment.
She hoped to redundant the argument by introducing the study\'s central claim.

definition: combining so as to complete or enhance each other
memoryTip: Complement (complete), not compliment (praise).
correctPassage: The two data sets proved complementary: one captured range, the other resolution.
wrongPassages: Reviewers called the copies complementary because each repeated the other word for word.
He sent a complementary note that attacked her methods without adding anything.
The fees were complementary, billed in full at the door with no offset.

definition: the state of being unable to exist or work together
memoryTip: In-compatible: the two will not run on the same system.
correctPassage: Software incompatibility kept the new sensors from talking to the old consoles.
wrongPassages: Their incompatibility was obvious once every trial produced identical, aligned results.
The treaty\'s incompatibility clause required both sides to adopt the same standard without conflict.
Chemists praised the reagents\' incompatibility after they mixed without any reaction or conflict.

definition: a continuous range with no sharp breaks between extremes
memoryTip: Continue-um — a stretch with no hard edges.
correctPassage: Historians now treat the period as a continuum rather than a sudden break with the past.
wrongPassages: The continuum split the sample into two non-overlapping, labeled bins.
She filed a continuum that ended the series and barred any further cases.
The statute drew a continuum so sharp that no intermediate case could exist.

definition: to deliberately avoid or keep away from
memoryTip: Sounds like “shoo” — you eschew what you refuse to touch.
correctPassage: The lab chose to eschew animal trials after a cheaper cell model proved reliable.
wrongPassages: She planned to eschew the archive by spending the month reading every folder.
The festival was designed to eschew local crafts by featuring them in every booth.
He eschewed dessert by ordering a second slice.

definition: to explain something in careful detail
memoryTip: Ex-pound: pound out the explanation until it is clear.
correctPassage: In the afterword she expounds the method that the novel only hints at.
wrongPassages: He managed to expound the theory in a single shrug that invited no questions.
Editors asked her to expound the chapter by cutting every clarifying example.
The sealed memo was meant to expound nothing and leave the policy unexplained.

definition: to save from loss, wreck, or destruction
memoryTip: Salvage = save what you can from the wreck.
correctPassage: Archivists worked through the night to salvage letters the flood had soaked.
wrongPassages: The wrecking crew arrived to salvage the library by demolishing the stacks.
She hoped to salvage the error by reprinting it on the front page.
Conservators salvage a painting when they discard the canvas and keep nothing.

definition: to accept without protest, even if unwilling
memoryTip: Quiet-esce: go quiet and go along.
correctPassage: After losing the vote, the minority caucus acquiesced in the revised timeline.
wrongPassages: She acquiesced by organizing a walkout and refusing to sign.
The board acquiesced only after rewriting every clause it had just rejected.
He acquiesced by voting no and walking out before the motion was called.

definition: to go beyond the usual limits of
memoryTip: Trans-cend: climb across the ceiling of the category.
correctPassage: The memoir transcends local history and becomes a study of how cities forget.
wrongPassages: The draft transcends nothing; it never leaves the narrowest departmental dispute.
She hoped to transcend the assignment by copying last year\'s outline.
Critics said the sequel would transcend the original by repeating it scene for scene.

definition: comparable in a relevant way; alike enough to compare
memoryTip: Analogy-ous: like enough to compare.
correctPassage: The insect\'s wing joints are analogous to a folding hinge, though the materials differ.
wrongPassages: The two systems were called analogous because no shared feature could be named.
She drew an analogous distinction that treated the cases as wholly unrelated.
Biologists labeled the traits analogous only after proving they were identical in origin and form.

definition: to make larger, more intense, or more noticeable
memoryTip: Magn-ify: raise the magnitude so you can see it.
correctPassage: The new lens can magnify surface cracks that inspectors previously missed.
wrongPassages: Soft lighting was used to magnify every blemish until the face looked nearly flawless.
Editors hoped to magnify the scandal by refusing to mention it in any edition.
The filter is designed to magnify impurities from the sample before analysis.

definition: to give particular importance or prominence to
memoryTip: Put it in the foreground — make it the thing you notice first.
correctPassage: The report foregrounds tenant testimony that earlier drafts had buried in an appendix.
wrongPassages: She chose to foreground the finding by deleting it from the abstract and title.
Designers foregrounded the logo by hiding it behind a full-bleed photograph.
The museum hoped to foreground the painting by storing it in an unlit vault.

definition: to exist or happen earlier than something else
memoryTip: Pre-date: come with an earlier date.
correctPassage: The irrigation canals predate the written records of the settlement.
wrongPassages: The sequel is said to predate the original, appearing a decade after it.
She hoped to predate the deadline by submitting the file two weeks late.
Archaeologists claimed the plastic fragments predate the site\'s earliest occupation.

definition: to attribute something to a particular cause or source
memoryTip: A-scribe: write the credit — or the blame — onto a source.
correctPassage: Later scholars ascribed the unsigned essays to a single government clerk.
wrongPassages: The lab ascribed the result by refusing to name any cause or source.
She ascribed the trophy on the mantel and walked away without comment.
Editors ascribed the error after demonstrating that no one in particular was responsible.

definition: to make use of, especially for one\'s own advantage
memoryTip: Exploit = put a resource to work — sometimes fairly, sometimes not.
correctPassage: As a defense, the butterfly exploits toxic compounds stored from the milkweed it eats.
wrongPassages: The species exploits the toxin by leaving the milkweed untouched all season.
Managers exploited idle machines by locking the shop and sending the crew home.
She hoped to exploit the archive by never opening a single folder.

definition: to divide into sharply opposing groups
memoryTip: Like polarized light — two opposite directions, no middle.
correctPassage: Coverage of the water plan polarized the town into shutoff and rationing camps.
wrongPassages: The workshop was designed to polarize volunteers by asking them to draft a shared statement.
After the vote, the issue polarized no one; every precinct returned the same margin.
Mediators hoped to polarize the talks by seating both sides at one table.

definition: to travel or extend across or through
memoryTip: Trans-verse: go across.
correctPassage: The survey team will traverse the canyon floor before mapping the north rim.
wrongPassages: They chose to traverse the mountain by remaining in camp for the entire season.
The fence was built to traverse nothing, stopping short of both property lines.
She traversed the chapter by skipping every section that crossed the main argument.

definition: free from a usual obligation or rule
memoryTip: Exempt = excused from the rule the others still follow.
correctPassage: Small farms are exempt from the reporting rule that applies to commercial processors.
wrongPassages: The handbook marked safety training exempt so that every employee had to complete it.
She was exempted from the fee by being charged double at the door.
Staff called every resident exempt even though the statute listed each one as subject to the same fine.

definition: to wipe out so that it can no longer be seen
memoryTip: Efface = erase the face of it.
correctPassage: Weather had begun to efface the inscription on the harbor wall.
wrongPassages: Conservators worked to efface the mural by restoring every faded line.
She hoped to efface her role by listing it first on the title page.
The new plaque was installed to efface the names so visitors could read them.

definition: impossible to read or interpret
memoryTip: In-decipherable: you cannot crack the cipher.
correctPassage: Water damage left the last page of the logbook indecipherable.
wrongPassages: The indecipherable handout spelled each step in numbered, plain English.
She preferred indecipherable prose that a first-year student could paraphrase on sight.
Editors called the diagram indecipherable after it made the process obvious to beginners.

definition: the quality of being uniform or all of the same kind
memoryTip: Homo-geneous quality — all one kind.
correctPassage: The sample\'s homogeneity made it a poor test of how the drug would work in a mixed population.
wrongPassages: Reviewers praised the city\'s homogeneity after documenting dozens of languages on one block.
The alloy showed homogeneity only where three metals remained visibly unmixed.
She sought homogeneity by recruiting every age, income, and schooling level she could find.

definition: arrogantly superior; scornfully proud
memoryTip: Haughty = high-and-mighty, looking down.
correctPassage: A haughty refusal to take questions undercut the mayor\'s claim of openness.
wrongPassages: Her haughty welcome put nervous guests immediately at ease.
The haughty volunteer stayed late to stack chairs and thanked everyone else first.
Reviewers called the speech haughty after he credited rivals and asked for correction.

definition: done with a minimum of effort or attention
memoryTip: Per-function-ory: just going through the function, not the spirit.
correctPassage: The inspector\'s perfunctory glance missed the cracked weld on the support.
wrongPassages: A perfunctory audit lasted three months and sampled every transaction.
She gave a perfunctory defense that cited overlooked data and rebuilt the model overnight.
The perfunctory rehearsal ran until each entrance could be timed to the second.

definition: to prove that something is genuine or valid
memoryTip: Make it authentic — show it is the real thing.
correctPassage: Specialists used pigment tests to authenticate the unsigned landscape.
wrongPassages: The lab moved to authenticate the relic by showing the paint was modern.
Forgers hoped to authenticate the letter by adding anachronistic watermarks.
Editors authenticated the quote by leaving the source unnamed.

definition: to make accustomed to something through repeated exposure
memoryTip: Habit-uate: turn it into a habit; get used to it.
correctPassage: After a month the birds habituated to the observation blind and resumed nesting.
wrongPassages: Sudden noise was used to habituate the herd, scattering it from the usual trail.
The program habituated newcomers by changing the rules every morning.
She hoped to habituate the jury with a single unrehearsed outburst.

definition: restraint in showing feelings or thoughts
memoryTip: Keep it in reserve — feelings held back.
correctPassage: Nothing in her reserve suggested anger; she simply declined to discuss the vote.
wrongPassages: His reserve poured out in a long, unfiltered speech about every slight.
She showed reserve by posting the argument on the laboratory door.
The reserve of the crowd was measured in chants that shook the hall.

definition: a difference, especially one that seems unfair
memoryTip: Dis-parity: the two sides are not a pair.
correctPassage: A growing disparity in broadband access left rural clinics unable to share records.
wrongPassages: The study found a disparity of zero: every district posted the same rate.
Managers celebrated the pay disparity after equalizing every salary band.
She hoped to disparity the two samples by matching them on every variable.

definition: the state of being kept secret or private
memoryTip: Confidential-ity: stays in confidence, not on the bulletin board.
correctPassage: Medical confidentiality barred the intern from discussing the case outside the team.
wrongPassages: The office treated confidentiality as a reason to post every file on the public site.
She signed a confidentiality notice that required her to brief the press daily.
Editors praised the leak\'s confidentiality after the draft appeared on every homepage.

definition: no longer produced or used; out of date
memoryTip: Ob-solete: no longer sold or used.
correctPassage: Punch-card readers are obsolete in labs that moved to solid-state storage.
wrongPassages: The obsolete protocol is still the required standard in every licensed clinic.
Designers called the prototype obsolete the morning it became the industry default.
She hoped to obsolete the method by making it the required textbook procedure.

definition: unoriginal; copied from something else
memoryTip: Derived from someone else — not a fresh idea.
correctPassage: Critics dismissed the score as derivative, echoing last decade\'s radio hits bar for bar.
wrongPassages: Reviewers called the method derivative because no earlier model could describe it.
Her derivative approach broke every convention the genre had relied on.
The theorem was labeled derivative after it introduced a proof no one had sketched.

definition: having many different parts or aspects
memoryTip: Many facets, like a cut gem.
correctPassage: The drought is a multifaceted crisis, hitting crops, power, and migration at once.
wrongPassages: The multifaceted rule had a single clause and no exceptions.
Editors praised the essay\'s multifaceted argument, which repeated one claim in one style.
He preferred multifaceted problems that reduced to a yes-or-no checkbox.

definition: to restrict something within limits
memoryTip: Circum-scribe: draw a circle around it and do not let it out.
correctPassage: New zoning rules circumscribe how tall any building near the river may rise.
wrongPassages: The charter was rewritten to circumscribe the agency by removing every spending cap.
She hoped to circumscribe creativity by handing artists a blank brief and no deadline.
Unlimited funding will circumscribe the lab by erasing each budget ceiling.

definition: full of energetic high spirits
memoryTip: Exuberant = energy overflowing the banks.
correctPassage: An exuberant crowd stayed after the recital to cheer each player by name.
wrongPassages: The exuberant eulogy was delivered in a whisper and ended in a long silence.
Reviewers called the monotone briefing exuberant because no one looked up.
Her exuberant caution kept every risk off the agenda and the room subdued.

definition: unable to notice fine differences; not discerning
memoryTip: Un-discerning: cannot tell good from bad.
correctPassage: An undiscerning audience applauded the unfinished draft as if it were the premiere.
wrongPassages: The undiscerning editor caught a one-word substitution no one else had noticed.
Her undiscerning tasting notes separated each vintage by soil, year, and barrel.
Judges were called undiscerning after ranking the entries with surgical precision.

definition: the act of casting inner feelings or ideas onto something outside the self
memoryTip: You project inner weather onto a character, a story, or someone else.
correctPassage: Without some projection of feeling onto the narrator, the chapter would read as a plain report and not as fiction.
wrongPassages: The chapter was praised for its projection after it reported facts and assigned no inner state to anyone.
He offered a projection that refused to place any motive or feeling outside himself.
Surveyors recorded a projection between the two property lines before building the fence.

definition: a cluster formed by many things gathering together
memoryTip: Aggregate = gather into one heap or group.
correctPassage: Researchers found an aggregation of octopuses along a single hydrothermal vent.
wrongPassages: The aggregation scattered the animals across isolated territories with no cluster in sight.
She filed an aggregation that split the sample into separate, non-overlapping cases.
After the herd dispersed, biologists still called the empty slope an aggregation.

definition: the process or state of becoming out of date
memoryTip: Obsolete-escence: the slide into unused.
correctPassage: Rapid software cycles have shortened the obsolescence of last year\'s devices.
wrongPassages: Builders chose granite for its obsolescence, expecting the memorial to last for centuries.
The design\'s obsolescence was praised because every part remained the current standard.
She valued the manuscript\'s obsolescence, confident that its ink would never fade.

definition: occurring at irregular intervals; not steady
memoryTip: Inter-mittent: it comes and goes, not a constant stream.
correctPassage: Intermittent radio contact forced the crew to repeat each instruction twice.
wrongPassages: The intermittent signal never dropped for the entire twelve-hour watch.
Engineers designed an intermittent current that flowed at one unchanging rate.
She preferred an intermittent schedule because every hour of the week was already booked.

definition: to turn upside down or reverse the order of
memoryTip: Invert = flip it: top becomes bottom, first becomes last.
correctPassage: The chemist inverted the flask so the last drops would run into the vial.
wrongPassages: She inverted the list by leaving every name in its original order.
The diagram was inverted so that up remained up and the sequence was unchanged.
Editors inverted the chapter by reprinting it exactly as submitted.

definition: a typical example or original model of a type
memoryTip: The first mold — later versions are copies of the archetype.
correctPassage: Holmes became the archetype for the brilliant, solitary detective who followed.
wrongPassages: Reviewers called the design an archetype because it matched no earlier model.
Biologists labeled the specimen an archetype when it shared none of the species\' known traits.
Her approach was so much an archetype that no convention or predecessor could describe it.

definition: a person or group that receives a benefit
memoryTip: The one who benefits — the money, the advantage, the will.
correctPassage: Rural clinics were the main beneficiaries of the new broadband grant.
wrongPassages: As chief beneficiary, the town paid the entire cost and received none of the service.
She named a beneficiary whose only role was to donate the funds, not receive them.
The beneficiary clause required the heir to forfeit every asset listed in the will.

definition: the direct opposite of something
memoryTip: Anti-thesis: the claim that sits directly across from yours.
correctPassage: His public humility was the antithesis of the boastful letters he sent at night.
wrongPassages: The sequel was the antithesis of the original, copying tone, plot, and cast.
She called the twins an antithesis because they agreed on every premise.
Editors praised the brief as the antithesis of the draft after changing nothing.

definition: to credit with; or to officially recognize as qualified
memoryTip: Put credit on someone — or stamp the school as official.
correctPassage: Later accounts accredit the design to an apprentice whose name never appeared on the patent.
wrongPassages: The board moved to accredit the program by stripping its license overnight.
Historians accredited the invention to no one after naming the inventor on every plaque.
She hoped to accredit the rumor by refusing to check a single source.

definition: to make an action or process easier
memoryTip: Facile = easy — facilitate clears the path.
correctPassage: Clear section headings facilitate comparison across the three case studies.
wrongPassages: New fees were introduced to facilitate applications by adding three extra forms.
The locked gate was meant to facilitate deliveries after hours.
Editors facilitated the argument by deleting every transitional sentence.

definition: to wander away from the main subject
memoryTip: Di-gress: step off the main path of the talk.
correctPassage: The lecturer would digress into family stories, then steer back to the data.
wrongPassages: She refused to digress, opening with a long aside that never returned to the thesis.
The brief was praised for how it would digress, staying on a single claim throughout.
He managed to digress by restating the title and sitting down.

definition: to bring into agreement or into the same line
memoryTip: A-line: get two things pointing the same way.
correctPassage: The foundation aligned its grants with the city\'s ten-year housing plan.
wrongPassages: The two agendas aligned only in the sense that they contradicted each other on every goal.
She hoped to align the beams by leaving them at opposing angles.
Negotiators aligned the drafts by discarding every shared clause.

definition: to offset a loss or make up for a lack
memoryTip: Compensation fills the hole — pay, or another advantage.
correctPassage: Longer growing days compensate for the region\'s thin, rocky soil.
wrongPassages: The bonus was meant to compensate workers by cutting the hours they had already been paid for.
Nothing was offered to compensate the delay; the schedule was simply shortened further.
They compensated the shortage by destroying what little stock remained.

definition: to include or contain as a part
memoryTip: En-compass: draw a compass circle that takes it all in.
correctPassage: The exhibit encompasses pottery, trade records, and a reconstructed kiln.
wrongPassages: The survey was rewritten to encompass the topic by omitting every related case.
Her study encompasses nothing beyond a single unused footnote.
Editors asked him to encompass the chapter by cutting it from the volume.

definition: to replace something older or less adequate
memoryTip: Super-sede: sit above the old rule and take its seat.
correctPassage: A digital filing system will supersede the paper ledgers next spring.
wrongPassages: The 1890 handbook was kept to supersede the updated code now in force.
She hoped to supersede the draft by reprinting it unchanged.
The obsolete rule was said to supersede the new statute that had just repealed it.

definition: given free of charge
memoryTip: Complimentary tickets are free; complementary parts complete each other.
correctPassage: Guests received complimentary transit passes for the weekend of the conference.
wrongPassages: The complimentary dinner was billed at full price on every receipt.
She sent a complimentary invoice that listed each unpaid fee.
Reviewers called the two data sets complimentary because one completed the other.

definition: involving risk or danger, especially to health or safety
memoryTip: Full of hazards — not safe to treat casually.
correctPassage: The warehouse stored hazardous solvents far from any open flame.
wrongPassages: Inspectors labeled the sealed water bottles hazardous after finding no risk at all.
The hazardous trail was chosen because every drop-off had already been fenced.
She described the empty playground as hazardous and opened it without a warning sign.

definition: absolutely necessary; cannot be done without
memoryTip: Not dispensable — you cannot throw this one away.
correctPassage: A working pump proved indispensable once the well was the town\'s only water source.
wrongPassages: The extra ribbon was called indispensable and then left unused in a drawer.
Reviewers found the chapter indispensable after cutting it without any loss of sense.
She treated the optional icebreaker as indispensable and canceled the safety briefing instead.

definition: a compromise in which one gain requires another loss
memoryTip: You trade one good for another — that swap is the trade-off.
correctPassage: Shorter wait times came with a trade-off: fewer specialists on each shift.
wrongPassages: The plan offered a trade-off in which every side gained and nothing was given up.
She filed a trade-off that required no exchange and changed no priority.
Engineers described a trade-off in which both speed and safety improved and no cost appeared.

definition: to list items one by one
memoryTip: Turn it into items — line by line, not one lump sum.
correctPassage: The auditor asked the office to itemize travel costs instead of reporting a single total.
wrongPassages: She chose to itemize the budget by combining every line into one unexplained figure.
The receipt was itemized as a single lump with no entries underneath.
Editors asked him to itemize the argument by dropping every supporting example.

definition: to renovate so that something looks new or works better
memoryTip: Re-furbish: polish it up and put it back in service.
correctPassage: The city will refurbish the 1920 station rather than replace it.
wrongPassages: Crews arrived to refurbish the hotel by stripping the wiring and leaving the rooms gutted.
She hoped to refurbish the manuscript by discarding every page.
The landfill was designed to refurbish furniture by burying it unopened.

definition: a limit or measurable factor that defines how something operates
memoryTip: The rails a system runs on — set the parameters, set the range.
correctPassage: Temperature was the one parameter the team could not hold steady overnight.
wrongPassages: They treated every parameter as optional and then claimed the system had no operating limits.
She filed a parameter that named no factor and set no boundary.
The open-ended brief was praised for its strict parameters after it listed none.

definition: a stand-in measure used when the real thing cannot be observed directly
memoryTip: A proxy stands in — you measure this because you cannot measure that.
correctPassage: Because the habitat itself was closed, biologists used soil organisms as a proxy for its health.
wrongPassages: Lab notes treated the thermometer reading as a proxy for that same reading.
The census was treated as a mere proxy after it recorded every household in person.
She hoped to proxy the instrument by using the instrument itself with no substitute.

definition: guidance given by a more experienced person over time
memoryTip: Mentor-ship: the ongoing help, not a one-off tip.
correctPassage: A year of mentorship helped the intern turn lab notes into a publishable methods section.
wrongPassages: The program advertised mentorship as a single unread pamphlet left on a chair.
The flyer promised mentorship and then assigned no advisor and no meetings.
His mentorship consisted of disappearing for the semester and answering no mail.

definition: the skill with which something is made, especially by hand
memoryTip: The craftsman\'s mark — skill you can see in the work.
correctPassage: The chair\'s joinery showed a craftsmanship that machine cuts rarely match.
wrongPassages: Reviewers praised the table\'s craftsmanship after noticing the legs had been glued on crooked and unfinished.
Mass-stamped trinkets were advertised for craftsmanship that required no skilled hand.
She measured the vase\'s craftsmanship in ounces rather than in how it was made.

definition: discouraging an action by making the consequences feared
memoryTip: Deter-ence: scare the act off before it starts.
correctPassage: Visible patrols were meant as deterrence, not as a response after a break-in.
wrongPassages: Unlocked doors with no posted penalty were described as deterrence.
They pursued deterrence by removing every penalty and publicizing the gap.
A welcome banquet was described as deterrence because guests felt entirely at ease.

definition: close, continuous watching of a person or place
memoryTip: Surveil-lance: keep watch, usually without being invited.
correctPassage: Harbor surveillance recorded the unregistered launch long before it reached the pier.
wrongPassages: The agency called it surveillance and then left the cameras off for the entire month.
She preferred surveillance that never looked at the subject or the site.
A single unread memo was filed as overnight surveillance of the warehouse.

definition: the process of converting information into a code to block unauthorized access
memoryTip: Encrypt = lock the message so outsiders cannot read it.
correctPassage: Patient files leave the clinic only after encryption, so a lost laptop is not an open record.
wrongPassages: The team used encryption by posting the passwords beside each file name.
Plain-text emails were praised for their encryption after anyone could read them.
She completed the encryption by leaving the draft on an unlocked shared drive.

definition: an object kept as a reminder of a person, place, or event
memoryTip: Memento = remember — a keepsake, not a forecast.
correctPassage: She kept a cracked ticket stub as a memento of the last show in the old hall.
wrongPassages: He bought a memento so he would have no reminder of the trip.
The blank form was filed as a memento of an event that had not yet been scheduled.
They discarded every photograph and still called the empty drawer a memento.

definition: a difference between things that should match
memoryTip: Dis-crepancy: the counts do not creep into agreement.
correctPassage: A discrepancy between the two ledgers sent the auditors back to the original invoices.
wrongPassages: The discrepancy was celebrated once both totals matched to the cent.
She noted a discrepancy of zero after every figure had already been reconciled.
Editors hoped to discrepancy the drafts by making the wording identical.

definition: an official public announcement
memoryTip: Proclaim-ation: said out loud, on the record.
correctPassage: The governor\'s proclamation set a day of mourning after the flood.
wrongPassages: A private whisper in a locked office was filed as a proclamation to the state.
She issued a proclamation by refusing to announce anything at all.
The sealed memo was treated as a proclamation even though it was never made public.

definition: the fact of happening again, especially something unwelcome
memoryTip: Re-current: it comes back around.
correctPassage: Doctors warned that a recurrence of the infection was likely without a longer course of treatment.
wrongPassages: The disease\'s recurrence was confirmed when it never appeared a second time.
She celebrated the one-time event as a recurrence that could not happen again.
Historians called the unique, unrepeated vote a recurrence of nothing in the record.

definition: close to the actual amount, but not exact
memoryTip: Approx-imate: in the neighborhood of the real number.
correctPassage: The map gives only an approximate shoreline, redrawn after each storm season.
wrongPassages: The approximate figure matched the official count to the last digit.
She demanded an approximate measurement that left no rounding and no range.
Auditors called the exact census approximate after it listed every household by name.

definition: to cooperate secretly in order to deceive
memoryTip: Col-lude: play on the same hidden side.
correctPassage: Prosecutors argued that the two firms had colluded to keep regional bids artificially high.
wrongPassages: The rivals colluded by publishing every offer and inviting outside bids.
She was said to collude when she reported the bid-rigging attempt the same afternoon.
Open hearings were described as a way to collude because nothing was hidden.

definition: to separate from; to deny connection with
memoryTip: Dis-associate: take your name off it.
correctPassage: After the leak, several sponsors moved to dissociate themselves from the campaign.
wrongPassages: She hoped to dissociate from the scandal by appearing in every advertisement for it.
The merger was designed to dissociate the two brands by printing both names on one label.
He dissociated the groups by seating them at a single shared desk.

definition: to show or confirm that something is true
memoryTip: Like a witness: attest that it really happened.
correctPassage: Independent counts attest that turnout rose in every urban precinct.
wrongPassages: The missing files were said to attest a claim no document could support.
She hoped silence alone would attest the figures no one had checked.
Editors moved to attest the article by removing every source note.

definition: gradual wearing down through sustained pressure or loss
memoryTip: It does not fall in a day — attrition grinds it down.
correctPassage: Staffing fell by attrition as retirements piled up and no replacements were hired.
wrongPassages: The army took the city in a single morning and still called the win a year of attrition.
A sudden hiring wave was described as attrition because the roster doubled overnight.
She planned an attrition that would restore every lost position in one week.

definition: no longer fashionable, useful, or current
memoryTip: Out of the mode — last season\'s method.
correctPassage: The firm abandoned outmoded inventory software that could not talk to the new registers.
wrongPassages: Designers called the prototype outmoded the week it became the industry standard.
Her outmoded methods are still required in every current training manual.
They kept the outmoded rule because it had just been written to replace the old one.

definition: an exact copy of something
memoryTip: Dupe-licate: the second one that matches the first.
correctPassage: She filed the original deed and kept a duplicate in the office safe.
wrongPassages: The duplicate differed from the original in every clause and date.
He called the unique manuscript a duplicate because no copy of it existed.
Editors asked for a duplicate that would rewrite the argument from scratch.

definition: a stated condition required as part of an agreement
memoryTip: A stipulated term — if you want the deal, this part is required.
correctPassage: One stipulation required the contractor to finish the roof before the first frost.
wrongPassages: The contract\'s only stipulation was that no condition of any kind would apply.
She added a stipulation that left every deadline optional and unenforced.
The open invitation was described as a stipulation because guests could come or not.

definition: smug satisfaction that keeps you from seeing a risk
memoryTip: Complacent = too pleased with yourself to notice the crack.
correctPassage: Early leads bred complacency, and the team stopped practicing before the final.
wrongPassages: Her complacency showed in nightly drills and a refusal to assume the lead was safe.
The audit praised the lab\'s complacency after it double-checked every safety seal.
He treated complacency as extra rehearsals scheduled the moment the first warning arrived.

definition: temporary; in place for now and subject to change
memoryTip: A provisional pass is for now — it can still be withdrawn.
correctPassage: A provisional license let the clinic open while the final inspection was scheduled.
wrongPassages: The provisional charter was carved in stone and barred any later revision.
They issued a provisional ruling that closed the case forever.
She called the permanent constitution provisional because it had already been ratified for good.

definition: the combining of different parts into a new whole
memoryTip: Syn-thesis: put the pieces together into one thing.
correctPassage: The building is a synthesis of glass walls and salvaged timber rather than a copy of either style.
wrongPassages: The synthesis separated each influence into its own sealed room.
Editors praised the essay\'s synthesis after it listed rival ideas and never joined them.
She achieved a synthesis by deleting every source except one.

definition: grand and impressive in appearance
memoryTip: It imposes itself on the eye — large, stately, hard to ignore.
correctPassage: An imposing tower of dark rock rises above the river and can be seen for miles.
wrongPassages: Reviewers called the shed imposing after noting how easily it disappeared behind a hedge.
The imposing cottage sat low and unremarkable at the end of the lane.
She preferred imposing furniture that no visitor would notice.

definition: to add untrue or extra details to make a story more interesting
memoryTip: Embellish the tale — decorate it past what happened.
correctPassage: Witnesses began to embellish the rescue until no two versions named the same street.
wrongPassages: Historians were asked to embellish the chapter by stripping every extra detail.
She embellished the minutes by recording only what had actually been said.
The report was embellished into a bare list of dates with no added color.

definition: impossible or extremely hard to notice
memoryTip: Im-perceptible: the senses cannot catch it.
correctPassage: The glacier\'s imperceptible daily creep added up to a mile over a century.
wrongPassages: An imperceptible flash lit the whole valley and woke every household.
The change was called imperceptible after every visitor remarked on it at once.
She preferred imperceptible type that could be read from across the room.

definition: something that differs from what is usual or expected
memoryTip: An-omaly: not the normal pattern.
correctPassage: One anomaly in the data — a midnight spike no model predicted — sent the team back to the sensors.
wrongPassages: Researchers called the regular, expected reading an anomaly and filed it as routine.
The anomaly matched every prior trial and surprised no one.
She hoped to anomaly the sample by forcing it onto the standard curve.

definition: to understand; or to arrest
memoryTip: Apprehend a meaning — or a suspect. Both are a kind of catching.
correctPassage: Few readers immediately apprehend how much the last paragraph undercuts the narrator.
wrongPassages: She failed to apprehend the warning and then explained every clause of it to the staff.
The brief was called impossible to apprehend even though every sentence was obvious on first reading.
He hoped to apprehend the theorem by leaving the lecture before it was stated.

definition: the quality of being brief and to the point
memoryTip: Terse-ness: short on purpose, not because you forgot the rest.
correctPassage: The terseness of the ruling left no clause open to a second reading.
wrongPassages: Reviewers praised the brief\'s terseness after it rambled for forty unfocused pages.
His terseness consisted of repeating every point three times with new examples.
She aimed for terseness by adding a long preface and two unused appendices.

definition: stubborn refusal to change one\'s mind or course
memoryTip: Obstinate-ness: planted, unmoved, even when asked nicely.
correctPassage: Her obstinacy on the deadline made any compromise over timing impossible.
wrongPassages: His obstinacy showed in how quickly he dropped the plan when the first objection arrived.
The committee\'s obstinacy consisted of rewriting the draft after every comment.
She was praised for obstinacy after yielding on each disputed clause.

definition: to cause or spur someone to do something
memoryTip: A prompt pushes the next action — it gets you started.
correctPassage: A chance field note prompted the team to measure surface temperatures on several fungi.
wrongPassages: A locked, unread file was said to prompt the measurements the team never took.
She hoped a reminder would prompt nothing and leave the work untouched.
Editors prompted the article by deleting the call to action.
